title: Circles & Parabolas
summary: A circle of radius $r$ centered at $(h,k)$ is $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$. A parabola $y=a(x-h)^2+k$ opens up or down with vertex $(h,k)$. Completing the square converts general equations to these standard forms.

circle.plain: All points a fixed distance from a center.

center and radius.plain: The circle's middle point and its size.

parabola.plain: A U-shaped curve, graph of a quadratic.

vertex.plain: The turning point of a parabola.
vertex.in_class: Max if it opens down, min if up.

axis of symmetry.plain: The vertical line through the vertex.

standard form.plain: The clean form revealing key features.

completing the square.in_class: Group and add $(b/2)^2$ to build squares.

concept_sections.heading: The circle equation
concept_sections.explanation: A circle centered at $(h,k)$ with radius $r$ is $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$. Read the center and radius straight from this form.

concept_sections.heading: General to standard (circle)
concept_sections.explanation: From $x^2+y^2+Dx+Ey+F=0$, complete the square in $x$ and in $y$ to recover the center and radius.

concept_sections.heading: The parabola in vertex form
concept_sections.explanation: $y=a(x-h)^2+k$ has vertex $(h,k)$ and axis $x=h$; $a$ sets width and direction (up if $a>0$).

concept_sections.heading: Finding the vertex from $y=ax^2+bx+c$
concept_sections.explanation: The vertex is at $x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$; plug in to get $y$. Or complete the square to reach vertex form.

concept_sections.heading: Graphing conics
concept_sections.explanation: Plot the center/vertex, use the radius or a few symmetric points, and sketch. Symmetry cuts the work in half.
math_steps: Plot the key point (center or vertex).

real_world_examples.title: GPS trilateration
real_world_examples.scenario: Distance from towers locates a phone.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Each 'within range $r$ of a tower' is a circle; intersections pin the position.

real_world_examples.title: Satellite dish shape
real_world_examples.scenario: A dish focuses signals to one point.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Its cross-section is a parabola, whose vertex form places the focus.

real_world_examples.title: Projectile arc
real_world_examples.scenario: A thrown ball traces a curve.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The path is a parabola; the vertex is the peak height.
